Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CTO - Orbis), Sofia Duarte (ML Eng - Orbis), James O'Neal (Lead SRE - Orbis)
summary: Discovery call to understand Orbis Intel's model selection needs across hosted/dedicated/private deployment options. Key topics: preferred open models, context length requirements (10k+), multilingual support, tool-calling/function calling for retrieval pipelines, and security/compliance constraints. Agreed next steps: share pricing and security docs, run benchmarks, and demo tool-calling integration.
topics: Open model comparisons (Llama variants, Mistral, Llama-3, Mistral-7B/30B, Mixtral)
Context length requirements (8k-32k; need reliable 10k+ kv-cache behavior)
Multilingual quality (Spanish, Portuguese, Mandarin, Arabic) and tokenization concerns
Tool-calling / function calling for chains: retrieval + structured outputs
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private: SSO, KMS, data residency, latency vs cost tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Alex from Redwood here, AE for the Orbis account, and Priya is our solutions engineer. Marcus, Sofia, James, thanks for your time.

[00:12] Marcus Lee: Yeah thanks Alex. We wanted to talk model selection — like what you recommend for our retrieval + RAG stacks, and whether hosted vs dedicated makes sense. We're also strict on data residency.

[00:28] Priya Nair: Hi all. Quick agenda: requirements, current infra, expected QPS, context lengths, and then model capabilities — multilingual and tool calling. Then we'll map to Redwood hosted/dedicated/private options.

[00:40] Sofia Duarte: To set context, our main workload is internal intelligence search across docs and code; we do a lot of long-context summarization and then downstream tool calls to our internal APIs. We often need about 8k to 12k tokens of context; for some use-cases we'd like 16k or more. Also important: Spanish and Portuguese support, occasional Mandarin and Arabic. Latency target is around 300-500ms for short responses, but batch jobs can be higher.

[01:10] James O'Neal: On the infra side, we're primarily on GCP, and we have a VPC we can connect to. For pilot we'd consider hosted with encrypted at rest, but for production we might want dedicated or private due to compliance.

[01:35] Alex Chen: Got it. When you say tool calls — are those function-calls like structured JSON outputs, or full external microservice calls?

[01:42] Sofia Duarte: Both — most commonly we want structured JSON back (like entity + metadata) that we then post to our internal API. And sometimes the model will call an internal tool to fetch user data, so function/tool calling support is mandatory.

[02:05] Priya Nair: Definitely supported — Redwood's runtime supports function/tool calling patterns and streaming structured outputs. One note: different open models have differing reliability on exact JSON outputs — we usually recommend a model that's been evaluated on structured output and you can fallback to a smaller deterministic model for post-processing.

[02:30] Marcus Lee: We are evaluating open models to avoid heavy per-token costs. Which models do you see customers using for long context and multilingual? We heard Llama-3 is good but pricey on some clouds, Mistral is fast, mixtral?

[02:50] Priya Nair: Right. Quick run-down: Llama-3 variants give strong instruction-following and multilinguality, especially with the 70B series, but require more GPU memory and are heavier. Mistral-30B (and recent Mistral variants) are very cost-effective and fast for many workloads but sometimes slightly weaker on low-resource languages. Mixtral or Mix models (we've seen community forks) can be good but vary. For consistent 10k+ contexts we recommend models that have native long-context support or using Redwood's KV cache and compilation kernel selection to make longer contexts practical.

[03:30] Sofia Duarte: How about tokenization — we're worried about character-based languages like Mandarin and also Spanish with lots of diacritics; will the model's tokenizer affect quality?

[03:42] Priya Nair: Yes — tokenization differences can change cost and accuracy. We run example prompts through candidate models as part of the benchmark; we'll check token counts and fidelity. For Mandarin we usually test with character-heavy prompts and sample documents.

[04:00] Marcus Lee: On the security front — SOC 2, SSO, KMS. For private deployment we'd need on-prem or VPC with customer-managed KMS.

[04:10] Alex Chen: We can provide SOC 2 and ISO artifacts for hosted and dedicated; for private deployments Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. There may be a platform fee for on-prem packages, which we can include in the pricing sheet.

[04:35] James O'Neal: Latency — you mentioned kernel selection and batching. For our interactive UI, we need token generation latency under ~500ms for 512-token generations. How consistent is that on dedicated vs. hosted?

[04:50] Priya Nair: Dedicated gives more predictable p99 latency because you reserve GPU capacity. Hosted is great for quick pilots and small volume, but you can see more variability under bursty load. We can show historical latency profiles for models and instance types in the pricing/benchmark doc.

[05:12] Sofia Duarte: About model fallbacks — we want graceful degradation if the big model is down or overloaded. Does Redwood route to smaller variants automatically?

[05:22] Priya Nair: Yes, Redwood's smart routing can fall back to compatible model variants by policy — e.g., if 70B Llama-3 is down, route to a 30B Llama-3 variant or a quantized Mistral variant. You can set policies by latency, cost, or SLA.

[05:40] Marcus Lee: For the benchmark I'd like to understand cost per 1M tokens for different model+deployment combos and also accuracy on our eval sets in Spanish/Portuguese.

[05:52] Alex Chen: We'll include TCO tables and examples for hosted vs dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit) vs private licensing. Also will list recommended quantization profiles for cost reduction and their expected quality delta.

[06:10] Priya Nair: One practical note — for JSON/tool-calling reliability we often recommend tuning prompts with structured output examples and using function signatures where supported by the model to improve deterministic outputs. We'll include those best practices in the follow-up doc.

[06:35] Sofia Duarte: Do you support code-runner style tool-calling? e.g., model returns a function name and args and Redwood triggers a webhook?

[06:45] Priya Nair: Yes, that's a common pattern. Redwood supports function-calling patterns and you can configure verified webhooks or proxying through your VPC. For private deployments you can keep all calls internal.

[07:05] James O'Neal: Any gotchas for GCP? We run everything there; network egress costs and peering to Redwood Dedicated zones matter.

[07:15] Alex Chen: We'll note region pairing and peering options. For Dedicated we can colocate in the same cloud region to minimize egress. For Private you remain in your VPC so egress isn't an issue.

[07:32] Marcus Lee: Ok, let's talk concrete model candidates. For 10k-16k context with good Spanish and Portuguese, what would you suggest?

[07:40] Priya Nair: My shortlist: 1) Llama-3-70B or a 34B variant (strong multilingual, high quality, heavier) 2) Mistral-30B-level variants with long-context fine-tuning (good latency/cost) 3) Falcon-40B-instruct-like forks for specific cases 4) Quantized Mixtral for cost-sensitive workloads. We'll test them on your eval set to pick the right tradeoff.

[08:10] Sofia Duarte: Do we need to worry about licensing for these open models if we run them in private?

[08:18] Alex Chen: Some models have specific licenses; we can include license guidance. For most open weights we can host in private, but we'll flag any restrictions.

[08:30] Marcus Lee: For the pilot, we want to a) validate multilingual accuracy b) validate function-calling reliability c) verify cost. What inputs do you need from us?

[08:40] Priya Nair: Sample documents, an eval set with ground truth in Spanish/Portuguese/Mandarin, and example function schemas. Also target QPS and an expected traffic profile (steady vs bursty).

[08:55] Sofia Duarte: We'll pull together the eval set and share it. Expect a mix of 1k short prompts and 300 long-context examples (~10k tokens).

[09:05] Alex Chen: Great. We'll plan a 1-week benchmark: run the shortlist of models under hosted and dedicated (if you opt to reserve) and provide cost/latency/accuracy tradeoffs.

[09:18] James O'Neal: If we go dedicated, how does autoscaling work? We want to handle spikes but keep baseline cost down.

[09:26] Priya Nair: Dedicated supports autoscale policies and burst capacity. You can configure baseline reserved GPUs and allow short bursts onto shared pools. We'll include recommended policies.

[09:42] Marcus Lee: Any red flags on data residency? We need logs and prompt traces to be audit-ready but not leave the region.

[09:50] Alex Chen: For hosted we offer region selection and can restrict logging retention. For dedicated and private we support region locks and full audit logs with customer-managed KMS. We'll include the details in the security pack.

[10:08] Sofia Duarte: One more thing on multilingual token costs: if tokenizers split Spanish differently, cost delta could be visible. Will your TCO sheet show tokenization differences across models?

[10:20] Priya Nair: Yes — our benchmark output will include token counts and cost per model per language.

[10:34] Marcus Lee: Cool. Anything else we should know before the next step?

[10:40] Alex Chen: We'll also include a short sample prompt/template library for structured outputs and a checklist for tool-calling security. Expect the email with docs and pricing by Friday.

[10:52] Sofia Duarte: Sounds good.

[11:00] Marcus Lee: Thanks all. Quick recap?

[11:03] Alex Chen: Recap — Redwood to send hosted vs dedicated pricing + security pack (Alex), schedule 1-week benchmark with sample data (Priya + Sofia), and follow-up demo on tool-calling (Priya). Action items and due dates noted.

[11:18] James O'Neal: I'll sync with infra on VPC peering requirements and share that with Priya.

[11:25] Alex Chen: Great, we'll follow up. Thanks everyone.

[11:30] (call ends)

Notes: Transcription has minor errors (names and model variants sometimes mis-heard). There were short crosstalk moments. References: "pricing sheet" (link to internal doc), "security pack" (link to Redwood security folder), and "benchmark plan" (shared Google Sheet).
